question: Do transformers generalize from facts stored in weights and examples supplied in context with the same inductive bias, or with rule- versus exemplar-based strategies?

key_findings.claim: On a controlled partial-exposure task, information learned into weights produces rule-based generalization.
key_findings.evidence: After training fixed stimulus-label mappings, held-out feature combinations are classified entirely using the single predictive feature, despite an alternative full-feature exemplar strategy fitting all observed combinations.

key_findings.claim: The same scratch-trained transformer generalizes from context by exemplar similarity when pretraining does not favor either strategy.
key_findings.evidence: For held-out BX after seeing AX, AW, and BW, models split predictions between labels associated with AX and BW, consistent with using both features and contrasting sharply with the weight-trained condition.

anchors.section: Generalization from in-context information and Figure 2

key_findings.claim: A naturally pretrained 70B language model is partly rule-based in context, and this tendency increases with model size.
key_findings.evidence: After controlling for an inherent color-over-shape bias, both color-predictive and shape-predictive partial-exposure prompts shift completions toward the sparse predictive dimension; 1B and 7B versions show progressively less of this shift, with 1B near the exemplar baseline.

key_findings.claim: Synthetic pretraining that explicitly rewards sparse-rule generalization can reverse the default contextual exemplar bias.
key_findings.evidence: Changing only the scratch model's pretraining task to require rule-based classification yields rule-based held-out predictions; increasing layers, heads, or classes without that data structure does not reproduce the effect.

method.core_idea: Create an ambiguity where both a sparse rule and exemplar similarity fit observed labels, then inspect the held-out combination that makes their predictions diverge.
method.mechanism: Train synthetic transformers either on fixed labels or few-shot sequences, run a two-feature partial-exposure query, repeat with shape/color words and nonsense labels in 1B-70B pretrained language models, calibrate against feature-bias controls, and modify pretraining to require rules.
assumptions: The partial-exposure response cleanly separates rule and exemplar strategies.
Synthetic fixed mappings isolate weight learning while random contextual mappings isolate in-context learning.
Shape/color word prompts are an informative proxy for general LLM induction.
Differences across pretrained sizes reflect scale despite possible data and training confounds.

techniques.role: Creates a held-out example where sparse-rule and exemplar predictions differ.
Manipulates whether task information is fixed during training or supplied only in the prompt.
Calibrates pretrained models' inherent preference for color or shape.
Tests whether rule-demanding data changes contextual generalization.

evaluations.setting: Scratch transformer with two-feature synthetic stimuli
evaluations.result: In-weights condition is fully rule-based; neutral few-shot in-context condition is fully exemplar-based
evaluations.baseline: Predictions implied by each cognitive model

evaluations.result: 70B is partly rule-based; rule-ness decreases with size and is near zero at 1B

evaluations.setting: Scratch transformer pretrained on rule-requiring sequences
evaluations.baseline: Few-shot pretraining where rule and exemplar strategies are equally valid

limitations: The central behavioral taxonomy reduces a continuum of possible algorithms to two stylized strategies.
Natural-language evidence uses only shape/color words, nonsense labels, and one pretrained model family.
Model-size comparisons may confound scale with data exposure, optimization, and capacity-dependent calibration.
The claim that natural language's sparse structure causes rule-ness is supported by an artificial intervention, not direct corpus manipulation.
Behavioral outputs do not identify the internal algorithm or representation.
failure_modes: Verbal-semantic priors dominate the intended abstract feature manipulation.
Prompt order, recency, or label-token frequency mimics rule-based response shifts.
A model interpolates between similarity and rules in a way the binary metric misclassifies.
Rule bias helps compositional tasks but amplifies a spurious sparse feature under distribution shift.
reusable_insights: Decide whether task knowledge belongs in weights or context partly by the desired generalization bias.
Use underspecified demonstrations and disambiguating tests to expose hidden feature preferences.
Manipulate pretraining distributions directly before attributing an emergent behavior to scale.
open_questions: Does the weights-context difference persist on natural tasks with controlled counterfactual training corpora?
Which attention or representation mechanisms implement exemplar and sparse-rule behavior?
How do instruction tuning, chain-of-thought, retrieval, and longer contexts shift the bias?

competitive_landscape.title: Data Distributional Properties Drive Emergent In-Context Learning in Transformers
competitive_landscape.relationship: direct predecessor from the same research line
competitive_landscape.difference: Chan et al. identify burstiness, rare classes, and Zipf structure that elicit ICL; the reviewed paper asks what generalization strategy the resulting contextual learner adopts.

competitive_landscape.title: What Can Transformers Learn In-Context? A Case Study of Simple Function Classes
competitive_landscape.difference: Garg et al. compare trained transformers with optimal estimators across function classes; the reviewed work distinguishes rule versus exemplar induction under deliberate ambiguity.

competitive_landscape.title: What learning algorithm is in-context learning? Investigations with linear models
competitive_landscape.difference: Akyürek et al. match in-context regression to gradient descent, ridge, and Bayesian estimators; the reviewed paper uses a cognitive rule/exemplar taxonomy for categorical generalization.

competitive_landscape.title: Measuring Inductive Biases of In-Context Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Si et al. scale underspecified-demonstration tests to multiple natural NLP datasets and spurious features; the reviewed paper offers the earlier controlled weights-versus-context contrast and data-structure intervention.

novelty_assessment: The paper's clean contribution is the within-architecture contrast between in-weight rule bias and contextual exemplar bias, plus evidence that pretraining structure can reverse the latter. The natural-language and scale interpretation is suggestive rather than causal because the prompt domain and model family are narrow and pretraining corpora are uncontrolled.
reviewer_notes: Read the complete short paper and appendices relevant to stimulus construction, controls, and model sizes. Primary arXiv records on emergent ICL, function-class learning, algorithmic ICL, and a later broader bias study were checked on 2026-08-23.
